                    ### Question
                    A 24-year-old woman, who is primiparous, suffers a miscarriage at 7 weeks of gestation. The anatomopathological study of the abortive remains indicates molar disease. We must inform you that:

                    ### Options
                    opa. The risk of a new molar gestation in a future pregnancy is 50%.
opb. You should not get pregnant until you have regular check-ups and a year of negative beta-HCG levels.
opc. No further monitoring is necessary if the evacuation of the trophoblastic tissue was complete.
opd. It is necessary to carry out periodic check-ups since in 40% of cases it will develop a gestational trophoblastic neoplasm.

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
In cases of molar pregnancy, the risk of recurrence in future pregnancies is increased but not as high as 50%; it is generally around 1-2%. After a molar pregnancy, it is standard to monitor beta-HCG levels until they return to normal to ensure complete resolution and to detect any potential development of gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN). It is recommended to avoid pregnancy until beta-HCG levels have been normal for 6-12 months. Complete evacuation of trophoblastic tissue does not eliminate the need for follow-up, as there is still a risk of GTN, though it is not as high as 40%. Regular follow-up is crucial to monitor for any complications or development of GTN.
